passage:
Dear Sonali,

I owe you the real version of Saturday, so here it is.

I said I had fever and couldn't come to your birthday. That was the first lie. The truth is my cousin had spare tickets to the kabaddi match, and I went.

When you showed me the photo on Monday, my face went hot and my brain just ran. I said the photo was from last year. Then, when you pointed at the date on the banner, I said you were checking up on me like a detective, and I walked off.

You didn't deserve that. You noticed something true, and I made you the problem, because owning up felt like shrinking in front of the whole class.

I'm sorry for skipping, sorry for the second story, and sorriest for turning on you. If you want to talk, I'll be on the library steps at lunch tomorrow.

Anjali

qa.q: What reason did Anjali first give for missing Sonali's birthday?
qa.a: Anjali said they had fever and couldn't come to the birthday.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when Sonali showed the photo, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Anjali felt panicked and ashamed: their face went hot, their brain just ran, and owning up felt like shrinking in front of the whole class.

qa.q: What could Anjali try the next time a lie is found out?
qa.a: Take one breath and admit the first lie straight away, instead of adding a second story or turning on the person who noticed.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt when called a detective?
qa.a: Sonali was probably hurt twice: first by the skipped birthday, then by being blamed for noticing something true.

grounding: Shows a teenager who, once caught, adds a second lie and attacks the person who noticed, because shame makes escape feel easier than admitting it.

passage:
Hi Pankaj bhaiya,

Something happened with Papa that I keep thinking about.

Last week he told me he had handed in my school trip form at the office. Two days later I was hunting for a charger in the car and found the envelope under the passenger seat, still sealed.

I held it up. For a second Papa started, "The office must have sent it back—" and then he stopped. He sat down on the front steps and said, "No. I forgot it, and I told you I'd done it because I felt silly. That was a lie. I'm sorry."

The next morning he took an hour off work and came to the school office with me to sort it out. The clerk said it was fine, just late.

Honestly, I was ready to be angry at him for days. Instead I felt oddly proud of him. I think I'll remember that envelope longer than the trip.

Pradeep

qa.q: Where did Pradeep find the trip form envelope?
qa.a: Pradeep found the envelope under the passenger seat in the car, still sealed.

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel after Papa admitted the lie?
qa.a: Pradeep had been ready to be angry for days, but instead felt oddly proud of Papa for saying it plainly.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Papa, and why?
qa.a: Stopping the excuse halfway, saying simply that he forgot and lied, apologising, and then fixing it at the school the next morning; it showed honesty instead of defending the lie.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Papa when the sealed envelope came out?
qa.a: Papa probably felt exposed and embarrassed, which is why he began an excuse before stopping to tell the truth.

grounding: Shows a parent caught in a small lie by their child who admits it simply and repairs it, and how much that teaches the child.

passage:
Bao cycled home from the rental shop in Utrecht with the lie riding alongside him. At closing, Emil had asked whether the brake checks on the six tandem bikes were done, and Bao had said yes. They weren't. He had spent that hour on his phone.

Tomorrow a school group was booked on those tandems. At the canal bridge he turned around.

Emil was still counting helmets. Bao's mouth was dry. "I told you the brakes were checked. I didn't check them. I'm sorry."

Emil set the helmets down and was quiet for a long moment. "Right. We check them now, together. And you're off the Saturday shift for a month."

They worked until nine under the workshop lamp. Two tandems had worn pads. Bao rode home tired and embarrassed, but his chest felt lighter than it had all evening. At the door Emil had said, "See you Tuesday."

qa.q: How many tandems had worn brake pads?
qa.a: Two tandems had worn pads.

qa.q: How did Bao feel on the ride home after owning up?
qa.a: Bao felt tired and embarrassed, but lighter than he had all evening, because the lie was no longer riding with him.

qa.q: What would you advise Bao if he is ever tempted to cover up a skipped job again?
qa.a: Say so at once and help put it right, as he did at the bridge; the earlier it is said, the less harm and the easier the repair.

qa.q: How might Emil see Bao after this evening?
qa.a: Emil likely trusts Bao more for coming back before anyone found out, which is why the month off Saturdays still ended with 'See you Tuesday'.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who admits a lie before being cornered, accepts the consequence, and keeps a second chance.

passage:
I sit across from Kalyani at the studio, so I saw most of it.

On Tuesday she told Joseph the printer had confirmed Friday for the catalogue. On Wednesday the printer emailed Joseph asking which Friday we meant. Nobody had called them.

Thursday's stand-up was quiet. Kalyani spoke first. "What I said on Tuesday was false. I hadn't called the printer. I lost track, and I didn't want to look behind. From now on I'll write a status only after I've confirmed it, and I'll flag delays the same day."

She didn't say it was the printer's fault. She didn't say Joseph shouldn't have checked.

Joseph nodded. "Thanks. I'll still ask for the confirmation emails for a while."

"That's fair," she said.

Her voice was steady, but she skipped lunch, and I can't say what was going on inside. It took about a month before Joseph stopped asking for the emails.

qa.q: What did Kalyani say she would do from now on?
qa.a: Kalyani said she would write a status only after she had confirmed it, and flag delays the same day.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have been feeling during the stand-up, and what hints at it?
qa.a: She was probably nervous and ashamed; she skipped lunch even though her voice stayed steady, though the narrator can only guess from these cues.

qa.q: Which parts of Kalyani's apology made repair possible?
qa.a: She named exactly what was false, said why, promised a concrete change, and accepted the checks as fair instead of making excuses or blaming Joseph.

qa.q: How does Joseph see Kalyani's apology at first?
qa.a: Joseph appreciates it but still wants the confirmation emails for a while, so his trust comes back slowly, over about a month.

grounding: Shows a person caught in a lie who names what was false, why it happened and what will change, and accepts that trust returns slowly, as seen by a coworker.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
Ritu, you asked why I didn't shout at your cousin yesterday. Sit, and let your Nani Gurleen tell you about Harleen.

We were fifteen, in the same class in Moga, practising a play for the school function. One Sunday Harleen told me she had fever and couldn't come. That evening my brother saw her at the mela, laughing on the swings.

The other girls wanted me to ask her in front of everyone on Monday, so she would squirm. I nearly did. Instead I waited by the canal after school and said, "I know you were at the mela. I'm not angry about the swings. Why did you feel you had to lie to me?"

She cried then. Her father had forbidden the play, and she was too ashamed to say so.

I told her, "You're still my friend. The lie was a bad choice, not a bad you."

We found her a backstage job her father allowed, and she never lied to me again.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen wait to talk to Harleen?
qa.a: Gurleen waited by the canal after school.

qa.q: What was Gurleen tempted to do at first, and why might she have felt that way?
qa.a: She felt hurt at being lied to by a close friend and nearly let the other girls make Harleen squirm in front of everyone.

qa.q: Which choice by Gurleen at fifteen turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Taking Harleen aside by the canal, saying what she knew and asking why, instead of a public confrontation; it left room for the truth and kept the friendship.

qa.q: What was it like for Harleen when Gurleen asked 'why' instead of accusing her?
qa.a: Harleen felt safe enough to cry and share the real reason, her father's ban on the play, because she wasn't being trapped or mocked.

grounding: Illustrates confronting a friend's lie privately: naming what is known, asking why it felt necessary, and separating the person from the act instead of shaming her.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
By Thursday Nadia had a small list in her head, and she sorted it on the tram home from the animal clinic in Lyon.

Monday: Aiko told Mrs Durand her knitted dog blanket was "perfect". It was lumpy. Nadia had smiled; that one cost nobody anything.

Tuesday and Wednesday: "Five minutes away!" when Aiko was clearly still at home. Annoying. Worth one honest word, not a war.

Today: the chart said the old beagle in kennel three had had his evening tablet. The tablet was still in the tray. It was the second time this month.

Nadia's stomach tightened. That wasn't smoothing anything over; an animal could suffer.

Two stops before her own, she got off and went back. She put the chart and the tray in front of Dr Morel, who gave the beagle his tablet at once. Then she found Aiko by the lockers. "I told Dr Morel about the chart. The late texts I can live with. This I can't."

qa.q: Where was the old beagle kept?
qa.a: The old beagle was in kennel three.

qa.q: What did Nadia feel when she saw the tablet still in the tray?
qa.a: Nadia felt alarmed; her stomach tightened because an animal could suffer, and it was the second time this month.

qa.q: Which of Nadia's choices matched the size of each lie?
qa.a: She let the kind blanket comment go, planned one honest word about the late texts, and took the repeated false chart to Dr Morel that same evening, setting a firm limit only where real harm was possible.

qa.q: How might Aiko experience Nadia's different reactions?
qa.a: Aiko may feel stung or defensive about the report, but the smile over the blanket and the calm plan about lateness show Nadia is not punishing every small untruth.

grounding: Shows an observer weighing someone's lies by their cost: a kind social untruth, an annoying pattern, and a repeated serious lie that gets a firm, proportionate response.

subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
passage:
"Chinmay, I talked to him every night for five months."
"I know, didi."
"Five months. And his photos belong to a wedding photographer in Indore. I found the real man's page today. Same balcony, same dog."
"Did you ever send him anything? Money, pictures?"
"No. He kept saying his account was frozen and maybe I could help. I kept saying later." She pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes. "How did I not see it?"
"Because he was good at it. That was his whole job, apparently. Not yours."
"I'm supposed to be the sensible one. I read everyone's rent agreements!"
"And you still said 'later' every single time he asked for money. That was your sense working."
Nandini gave a wet, shaky laugh. "It doesn't feel like sense. It feels stupid."
"Feeling stupid isn't the same as being stupid. Block him, and we'll report the profile tonight. Then chai."
"Okay. Tonight."

qa.q: Whose photos had the man been using?
qa.a: His photos belong to a wedding photographer in Indore.

qa.q: What is Nandini feeling as she talks to Chinmay?
qa.a: Nandini feels ashamed and foolish, doubting her own judgement because she is 'supposed to be the sensible one'.

qa.q: What small steps does Chinmay suggest for tonight?
qa.a: Block him and report the profile tonight, then sit together over chai, so Nandini acts on it and isn't left alone with the shame.

qa.q: How does Chinmay see what happened to Nandini?
qa.a: Chinmay sees her as the target of a practised deceiver, not a fool, and points out that her repeated 'later' to money requests was good sense.

grounding: Shows a person who finds she was deceived for months feeling foolish, while Chinmay reframes it: being fooled by someone practised at it is not a personal failing.

subtype: Telling the truth to a friend at a price [Actor]
passage:
The microscope lens hit the lab floor with a small, awful click. Deepak stared at the crack running across it.

Ganga swept the glass bits into her palm. "Put it back in the box. It was already loose, okay? We all say that."

The other three nodded fast. Nobody wanted Monday detention.

Deepak put the box back on the shelf. His hands were shaking. All through the period the story sat in his stomach like a stone.

When the bell rang, he went to the lab in-charge's desk. "Sir, I dropped the microscope. It wasn't loose. It was me."

Mr Bhaskar looked at him for a long moment. "Thank you for telling me. You'll help me clean the lab after school this week."

At lunch Ganga sat at another table and didn't look up. Deepak ate alone, cheeks hot. But on the walk home, for the first time that day, he could breathe all the way in.

qa.q: What did Ganga tell the group to say about the microscope?
qa.a: Ganga said it was already loose, and they would all say that.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel while the cover story sat with him through the period?
qa.a: Deepak felt anxious and guilty; his hands were shaking and the story sat in his stomach like a stone.

qa.q: What could Deepak try tomorrow to ease things with Ganga without backing down?
qa.a: Talk to Ganga calmly, say he spoke only about his own drop and didn't want anyone in trouble, while staying clear that telling the truth was right.

qa.q: Why might Ganga react differently from Deepak?
qa.a: Ganga was probably scared of the detention and felt let down by the group plan falling apart, so she sat apart instead of seeing his choice as brave.

grounding: Shows a teenager owning up to breaking something despite a group cover story, paying with cleaning duty and a classmate's cold shoulder, and gaining lasting self-respect.

passage:
The group chat lit up at one in the morning. Vera had the answers for the statistics coursework, bought from a student who had taken the module last year. "Just change the wording," Vera wrote. "Everyone's doing it."

Zeynep sat in the kitchen of the shared flat in Izmir, a cold cup of linden tea beside her laptop and question four still broken. Eleven people reacted with a thumbs up.

She typed "thanks, I'll pass", deleted it twice, then sent it.

The next week the marks came out. Vera and most of the others had high marks. Zeynep had a middling pass and a note: "Q4 method wrong, but reasoning clearly shown."

The fear arrived fast: scholarship reviews, rankings, being the slow one. Under it sat something steadier. On Friday, when the lecturer went through question four in the tutorial, Zeynep followed every step, and she was the one who asked the question half the room needed.

qa.q: How many people reacted with a thumbs up?
qa.a: Eleven people reacted with a thumbs up.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Zeynep have when the marks came out?
qa.a: She felt fear about scholarship reviews, rankings and being the slow one, and under it a steadier calm about having done her own work.

qa.q: What went well in Zeynep's choice, and what did it cost?
qa.a: She kept her work her own and truly learned the method, which showed in the tutorial; the cost was a lower mark than those who used the bought answers.

qa.q: How might Vera see Zeynep's 'I'll pass'?
qa.a: Vera might think Zeynep is being stiff or overly careful, especially since the bought answers earned high marks.

grounding: Shows a young adult turning down bought coursework answers while others benefit, feeling the fear of falling behind alongside a clean conscience.

subtype: Admitting a mistake at work or college [Actor]
passage:
The evening milk had been poured and the farmers had gone home when Ganga noticed it. In the register at the Rampur dairy collection centre she had written Shankar Kaka's cans as eight litres. The slip on the spike said eighteen.

Nobody would check before Saturday's payments. If anyone noticed later, she could blame the smudged slip.

Her fingers were cold. She carried the register to Sonali-didi, who was locking the cooling tank.

"Didi, I wrote eight instead of eighteen for Shankar Kaka. It's my mistake."

Sonali's voice rose so sharply that the helper boy looked over. "Do you know how that looks if he complains first? Twice you've been careless this month!"

Ganga stood and took it, face burning. They corrected the entry together, and Sonali signed beside it.

A month later, when Sonali went away for her sister's wedding, it was Ganga she left with the register and the keys.

qa.q: What did the slip on the spike say?
qa.a: The slip on the spike said eighteen.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel as she carried the register to Sonali?
qa.a: Ganga was scared, her fingers cold, yet determined to report her own mistake before anyone else found it.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Ganga made an entry error; reporting it at once and correcting it together, with Sonali's signature, fixed it before it could hurt Shankar Kaka's payment.

qa.q: How does Sonali's view of Ganga change by a month later?
qa.a: Though Sonali scolded her, she came to trust Ganga enough to leave her the register and the keys during the wedding.

grounding: Illustrates a young woman reporting her own error before it is found, facing a scolding, and earning more trust afterwards than silence would have protected.
